SECTIONS.title: What is abnormal? History of the field
ideas: Comer’s working definition uses the four Ds: deviance (different from the norms of the culture), distress (unpleasant and upsetting to the person), dysfunction (interferes with daily functioning) and danger (to self or others). No single D is enough on its own, and every one depends on context and culture.
Ancient views: trephination (holes chipped in the skull, possibly to release spirits); Hippocrates explained abnormality as an imbalance of four bodily humors (a somatogenic, natural explanation).

Middle Ages in Europe: demonology returned, with exorcism, and outbreaks of mass madness (tarantism, lycanthropy). Renaissance: Johann Weyer argued the mind can be sick like the body; asylums spread (London’s Bethlehem Hospital, “Bedlam”), often as warehouses.

Moral treatment (19th century): Philippe Pinel unchained patients in Paris, William Tuke founded the York Retreat, Benjamin Rush brought it to the US and Dorothea Dix campaigned for state hospitals. It declined as hospitals became overcrowded and underfunded.

Early 20th century: the somatogenic perspective gained ground when general paresis was traced to syphilis; the psychogenic perspective grew from Mesmer, Charcot, Breuer and Freud (hypnotism, then psychoanalysis). From the 1950s, antipsychotic drugs enabled deinstitutionalization, and today most treatment is outpatient, often under managed care.

SECTIONS.title: Models of abnormality
ideas: Biological model: abnormality comes from the brain and body: brain anatomy, neurotransmitters (serotonin, dopamine, GABA, norepinephrine, glutamate), hormones, genes, evolution and infection. Treatments: psychotropic drugs, electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), brain stimulation and, rarely, psychosurgery.

Psychodynamic model (Freud and successors): unconscious conflicts between the id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle) and superego (conscience), managed by defense mechanisms such as repression, denial, projection, rationalization and displacement. Therapy uses free association, interpretation of resistance and transference, dream interpretation, catharsis and working through; modern short-term psychodynamic therapies focus on one problem.

Cognitive-behavioral model: behaviors are learned through operant conditioning (rewards and punishments), modeling and classical conditioning (a neutral stimulus paired with one that produces a response). Cognitions matter too: Beck’s and Ellis’s maladaptive assumptions, automatic thoughts and illogical thinking. CBT changes both; the new wave (acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness) teaches people to accept thoughts rather than fight them.

Humanistic-existential model: people strive to self-actualize. Carl Rogers’s client-centered therapy offers unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy and genuineness; Perls’s gestalt therapy uses role-play and skillful frustration; existential therapy stresses freedom, choice and responsibility.

Sociocultural model: abnormality grows out of families, social roles and labels, social networks and culture (race, gender, poverty, discrimination). Treatments: group, family (family systems theory), couple and community treatment with primary, secondary and tertiary prevention, plus culture-sensitive therapy. The developmental psychopathology and biopsychosocial (diathesis–stress) views integrate the models: a predisposition plus a stressor.

SECTIONS.title: Assessment, diagnosis and treatment
ideas: A good assessment tool is standardized (same procedure and norms for everyone), reliable (consistent: test-retest and interrater reliability) and valid (measures what it claims: predictive, concurrent, content and face validity; face validity alone proves little).

Tools: clinical interviews (unstructured or structured), projective tests (Rorschach inkblots, the Thematic Apperception Test, sentence completion, drawings; low reliability and validity), personality inventories such as the MMPI (MMPI-2 and MMPI-3, with validity scales), response inventories, psychophysiological tests, neuropsychological tests and intelligence tests.
Clinical observation can be naturalistic, analog (in an artificial setting) or self-monitoring. Problems include observer drift, observer bias and reactivity (people act differently when watched).

Diagnosis uses a classification system. In the US that is the DSM-5-TR (2022), which lists criteria, duration and specifiers; many countries use the WHO’s ICD-11. Diagnoses can be categorical (present or absent) or dimensional (rated by severity), and labels can stigmatize, as Rosenhan’s 1973 “pseudopatient” study argued.

Treatment research asks whether therapy helps: overall, therapy clearly beats no treatment. The rapprochement movement looks for common factors shared by effective therapies, and empirically supported treatments are those tested with controlled trials. Beware the uniformity myth, the idea that all therapists and clients are alike.

SECTIONS.title: Anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and related disorders
ideas: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD): excessive, hard-to-control worry about many things, more days than not for at least 6 months, with at least 3 of 6 symptoms in adults (restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep trouble). Explanations include the sociocultural view (dangerous environments), cognitive views (metacognitive theory, intolerance of uncertainty, avoidance theory) and biology (GABA, benzodiazepines).

Phobias: specific phobia (a particular object or situation) and agoraphobia (fear of places where escape could be hard, in at least 2 of 5 situation types), both lasting 6 months or more. Behaviorists explain phobias through classical conditioning and modeling, kept alive by avoidance; the treatment is exposure (systematic desensitization, flooding, modeling).
Social anxiety disorder: intense fear of social or performance situations where one could be judged, lasting 6 months or more. Treated with exposure, social skills training, CBT and antidepressants.

Panic disorder: recurrent, unexpected panic attacks (a surge of intense fear peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms) followed by at least a month of worry about more attacks or changed behavior. Explained by the locus coeruleus and norepinephrine, plus the cognitive idea of misinterpreting body sensations; treated with antidepressants and CBT with interoceptive exposure.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD): obsessions (intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images) and/or compulsions (repetitive acts done to reduce distress) that take time (often over an hour a day) or cause distress. First-line treatments: exposure and response prevention (ERP) and SSRIs; serotonin and orbitofrontal-caudate circuits are implicated. Related disorders include body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, trichotillomania and excoriation.

SECTIONS.title: Disorders of trauma and stress
ideas: The stress response uses two systems: the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic arousal, the fight-or-flight response) and the HPA axis (hypothalamus → pituitary → adrenal glands, releasing cortisol).

Acute stress disorder and PTSD both follow exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence (experienced, witnessed, learned about in a close person, or repeated exposure to details at work). Acute stress disorder lasts 3 days to 1 month; PTSD lasts more than a month and can have delayed expression (full criteria met 6 months or more later).

PTSD symptoms fall in four groups: intrusion (memories, nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance of reminders, negative changes in thinking and mood (blame, detachment, inability to feel positive emotions) and arousal and reactivity (hypervigilance, startle, sleep problems, irritability).

Risk factors include biological differences (cortisol, a smaller hippocampus), personality, childhood adversity, weak social support and how severe the trauma was. Most people exposed to trauma do not develop PTSD.

Treatments with good evidence include trauma-focused CBT (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy) and EMDR; antidepressants help some people. Psychological debriefing right after a disaster has not been shown to prevent PTSD and may even hurt. Adjustment disorder covers emotional or behavioral symptoms that begin within 3 months of an ordinary stressor.

SECTIONS.title: Depressive disorders
ideas: A major depressive episode needs 5 or more of 9 symptoms over the same 2 weeks, including depressed mood or loss of interest (anhedonia). The others are weight or appetite change, sleep change, psychomotor agitation or slowing, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, and thoughts of death or suicide.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is depressed mood most days for at least 2 years (1 year in children and teens). Also in the chapter: premenstrual dysphoric disorder and disruptive mood dysregulation disorder in children.

Biological explanations: genetic risk, low activity of serotonin and norepinephrine (the classic monoamine hypothesis, now seen as incomplete), cortisol and the HPA axis, and brain circuits including the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus and amygdala.

Psychological explanations: Freud’s symbolic loss; Lewinsohn’s behavioral theory of fewer rewards; Beck’s cognitive triad (negative views of self, world and future) and errors in thinking; learned helplessness (Seligman) and the attribution version (internal, global, stable explanations for failures); rumination.

Treatments: antidepressants (SSRIs such as fluoxetine; SNRIs; older tricyclics and MAO inhibitors), CBT and behavioral activation, interpersonal psychotherapy, ECT for severe or treatment-resistant cases, and newer options such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and ketamine-based treatment.

SECTIONS.title: Bipolar disorders
ideas: A manic episode is a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive or irritable mood and increased energy lasting at least 1 week (any length if hospitalized), with 3 or more symptoms (4 if the mood is only irritable): inflated self-esteem, less need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, distractibility, more goal-directed activity and risky behavior. It causes marked impairment, hospitalization or psychosis.
A hypomanic episode has the same kinds of symptoms for at least 4 days but is not severe enough to cause marked impairment or hospitalization, and has no psychotic features.

Bipolar I disorder: at least one manic episode (depressive episodes are common but not required). Bipolar II disorder: at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode, and never a full manic episode. Cyclothymic disorder: at least 2 years (1 in youth) of many hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria.
Causes: bipolar disorders are among the most heritable disorders; theories involve neurotransmitter activity, ion activity in neurons, brain structure and genetics.

Treatment centers on mood stabilizers: lithium (needs blood-level monitoring) and anticonvulsants such as valproate and lamotrigine, plus second-generation antipsychotics. Psychotherapy (psychoeducation, family therapy, CBT, a regular sleep routine) adds to medication but does not replace it.

SECTIONS.title: Suicide
ideas: If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 (the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or contact MSU Counseling at (406) 994-4531. Asking someone directly about suicide does not plant the idea; it opens the door to help.

Shneidman described people who end their lives by intent: death seekers (clear intention), death initiators (believe they are hastening an inevitable death), death ignorers (believe death is not the end) and death darers (ambivalent, acting in ways that risk death). Subintentional deaths are those in which a person plays an indirect or hidden role.

Durkheim tied suicide to a person’s relationship with society: egoistic (little connection), altruistic (so connected they sacrifice themselves) and anomic (after a sudden change in social structure or one’s place in it).

Risk factors include past attempts, depression and other disorders (bipolar disorder, substance use, schizophrenia, borderline personality disorder), hopelessness, access to lethal means (especially firearms), stressful events, and modeling (suicide contagion after publicized deaths). Men die by suicide more often, while women attempt it more often, largely because of differences in method.

Prevention and treatment: crisis lines and 988, safety planning, reducing access to lethal means, treating the underlying disorder, and therapies with evidence for reducing suicidal behavior such as DBT and CBT for suicide prevention. Some antidepressants carry an FDA warning about increased suicidal thinking in people under 25, so they are monitored closely.

SECTIONS.title: Disorders featuring somatic symptoms
ideas: Factitious disorder: a person fakes or induces illness to take on the sick role, with no obvious external reward (formerly Munchausen syndrome); factitious disorder imposed on another does this to someone else, often a child. Malingering is faking for an external gain (money, avoiding work) and is not a mental disorder.

Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder): a neurological-seeming symptom (paralysis, blindness, seizures, loss of feeling) that is inconsistent with known neurological disease. Symptoms such as glove anesthesia do not follow the body’s nerve pathways.

Somatic symptom disorder: one or more distressing bodily symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviors about them (usually lasting over 6 months). Illness anxiety disorder: preoccupation with having or getting a serious illness despite few or no symptoms, lasting at least 6 months.

Explanations: psychodynamic ideas of converted conflict and primary and secondary gain; cognitive-behavioral ideas of misreading normal body sensations and rewarding illness behavior; biological findings of altered brain activity in functional disorders.

Treatment: insight therapy, exposure and response prevention for health worry (no checking or reassurance-seeking), CBT that reframes body sensations, and suggestion or reinforcement of healthy behavior. Psychophysiological disorders (such as some ulcers, asthma or hypertension linked to stress) are real medical illnesses that stress and psychology can worsen.

SECTIONS.title: Eating disorders
ideas: Anorexia nervosa: restricting food leads to significantly low body weight, with intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted view of body shape or weight. Types: restricting and binge-eating/purging. Adult severity uses BMI: mild 17 or above, moderate 16–16.99, severe 15–15.99, extreme below 15. It carries the highest death rate of the eating disorders.

Bulimia nervosa: recurrent binges (a large amount of food in a short time with a sense of losing control) followed by compensatory behavior (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, excessive exercise), both at least once a week for 3 months, with self-worth tied to shape and weight. Weight is often in the normal range.

Binge-eating disorder: recurrent binges at least once a week for 3 months with marked distress, but without regular compensatory behavior. It is the most common eating disorder. ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder) involves restricted eating without body-image concerns.

Explanations form a multidimensional risk picture: psychodynamic and cognitive factors (Hilde Bruch’s ideas about ineffective parenting and a lack of self-awareness), depression, biological factors (the hypothalamus and weight set point, genetics, serotonin), societal pressure toward thinness, family environment, and racial, cultural and gender differences.

Treatment: first restore weight and nutrition when health is at risk, then address thinking and relationships. Family-based treatment (the Maudsley approach) has strong support for adolescents with anorexia; CBT is the leading treatment for bulimia and binge-eating disorder; antidepressants help some bulimia cases.

SECTIONS.title: Substance use and addictive disorders
ideas: DSM-5-TR uses one substance use disorder with 11 possible criteria in four groups (impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological criteria: tolerance and withdrawal). Severity: mild 2–3 criteria, moderate 4–5, severe 6 or more, within a 12-month period.

Depressants slow the central nervous system: alcohol (increases GABA effects; long-term heavy use can cause Korsakoff’s syndrome from thiamine deficiency, and fetal alcohol syndrome in pregnancy), sedative-hypnotics (benzodiazepines) and opioids (bind endorphin receptors; overdose slows breathing and is reversed by naloxone).

Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, caffeine, nicotine) increase dopamine and norepinephrine activity. Hallucinogens (LSD, psilocybin) alter perception. Cannabis acts on cannabinoid receptors; THC potency has risen sharply over recent decades.

Causes: the brain’s reward pathway (dopamine, nucleus accumbens) and reward-deficiency ideas, genetics, tolerance-producing brain changes, operant and classical conditioning, expectancies, and sociocultural factors such as stress, poverty and family use.

Treatment: detoxification; agonist substitution (methadone or buprenorphine for opioids), antagonists (naltrexone) and aversion therapy; CBT and relapse prevention; contingency management; motivational interviewing; self-help groups (AA). Gambling disorder is the only non-substance addictive disorder in the DSM; internet gaming disorder is listed as a condition for further study.

SECTIONS.title: Technology and mental health
ideas: This is a lecture topic, not a textbook chapter, so the lecture notes are the source for the exam. The core scientific question is correlation versus causation: heavy screen or social media use is associated with poorer well-being, but the direction and size of the effect are debated.

Large studies generally find small average associations between screen time and teen well-being; effects seem to depend on what people do (passive scrolling, comparison, cyberbullying and lost sleep look worse than active connection).

Internet gaming disorder appears in DSM-5-TR Section III as a condition for further study, not an official diagnosis; the WHO’s ICD-11 does include gaming disorder. Gambling disorder is the only official behavioral addiction in the DSM.

Technology also changes treatment: telehealth therapy (much expanded since 2020), internet-delivered CBT, mental health apps with mixed evidence, text-based crisis services and 988, and virtual reality for exposure therapy.

Evaluate claims like a scientist: ask whether a study was correlational or experimental, whether a third variable (such as loneliness or poor sleep) could explain the link, and whether the effect is large enough to matter.

SECTIONS.title: Sexual dysfunctions, paraphilic disorders and gender variations
ideas: The human sexual response cycle (Masters and Johnson, with Kaplan adding desire): desire, excitement (arousal), orgasm and resolution. Sexual dysfunctions disrupt a phase: desire (male hypoactive sexual desire disorder, female sexual interest/arousal disorder), excitement (erectile disorder), orgasm (delayed ejaculation, female orgasmic disorder, premature ejaculation) and pain (genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder). Most require about 6 months and significant distress.

Causes mix biological factors (hormones, blood flow, medications such as SSRIs, alcohol), psychological factors (performance anxiety, the “spectator role”, depression) and sociocultural factors (relationship problems, culture and trauma).
Treatment: sex therapy combines education, reducing performance anxiety through sensate focus, communication training, and specific techniques; medications such as sildenafil treat erectile disorder.

A paraphilia is an intense, recurring atypical sexual interest; it becomes a paraphilic disorder only when it causes the person distress or impairment, or involves harm or risk of harm to others (such as non-consenting people), usually for at least 6 months. Examples include voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, frotteuristic and pedophilic disorders.

Gender dysphoria is distress from a marked incongruence between one’s experienced gender and assigned gender lasting at least 6 months. Being transgender or gender-diverse is not itself a disorder; the diagnosis centers on distress, and it remains debated. Care may include psychotherapy, social transition and gender-affirming medical care.

SECTIONS.title: Schizophrenia and psychosis
ideas: Schizophrenia needs 2 or more of 5 symptoms for a significant part of a month (at least one of the first three): delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms. Continuous signs must last at least 6 months, with a decline in functioning. Lifetime prevalence is about 1 in 100.

Positive symptoms are excesses: delusions (persecution, reference, grandeur, control), hallucinations (most often auditory), formal thought disorder (loose associations, neologisms) and inappropriate affect. Negative symptoms are deficits: alogia (poverty of speech), blunted or flat affect, avolition (loss of motivation), social withdrawal. Psychomotor symptoms include catatonia.

Related disorders by duration: brief psychotic disorder (at least 1 day but under 1 month), schizophreniform disorder (1 to 6 months), schizophrenia (6 months or more), schizoaffective disorder (a mood episode plus psychosis, with at least 2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms) and delusional disorder (delusions for at least 1 month without other psychotic symptoms).

Biological causes: strong genetic risk (roughly half of identical twins share it), the dopamine hypothesis (too much dopamine activity in some pathways, supported by antipsychotics blocking D2 receptors and amphetamines worsening symptoms), glutamate, enlarged ventricles and reduced brain volume, and prenatal or viral factors.

Psychological and sociocultural factors: the diathesis–stress model; high expressed emotion in families (criticism, hostility, over-involvement) predicts relapse; social labeling; and cultural differences in course and outcome. Double-bind theory and “schizophrenogenic mothers” have been discredited.

SECTIONS.title: Treating schizophrenia and other severe disorders
ideas: Before the 1950s, institutional care was the norm; milieu therapy (a therapeutic community) and the token economy (operant rewards for desired behaviors) improved hospital care.

First-generation antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, haloperidol) block dopamine D2 receptors and reduce positive symptoms. Side effects include extrapyramidal effects (Parkinsonian symptoms, dystonia, akathisia), tardive dyskinesia (involuntary movements that can be permanent) and, rarely, neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics (clozapine, risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) cause fewer movement side effects and may help some negative symptoms, but can cause weight gain, diabetes and other metabolic problems. Clozapine works for many treatment-resistant patients but requires blood monitoring for agranulocytosis.

Psychotherapy helps alongside medication: CBT for psychosis (testing beliefs about voices), family therapy and psychoeducation (lower expressed emotion, fewer relapses), social skills training and supported employment.

Deinstitutionalization moved people out of hospitals; effective community mental health includes coordinated care, short-term hospitalization, halfway houses and assertive community treatment. Where community care was underfunded, many people became homeless or incarcerated. Coordinated specialty care for a first episode of psychosis improves outcomes.

SECTIONS.title: Narcissism
ideas: This is a lecture topic, so the lecture notes come first. Narcissism ranges from a normal personality trait (measured, for example, by the Narcissistic Personality Inventory) to narcissistic personality disorder (NPD), a Cluster B disorder.

NPD needs 5 or more of 9 features, starting by early adulthood: grandiosity, fantasies of unlimited success or power, believing one is special, needing excessive admiration, entitlement, exploiting others, lacking empathy, envy (or believing others envy one) and arrogance.
Researchers distinguish grandiose narcissism (bold, dominant, attention-seeking) from vulnerable narcissism (defensive, easily hurt, secretly grandiose, prone to shame and anxiety).

Explanations: psychodynamic accounts of cold parenting or over-praise (Kohut, Kernberg), cognitive-behavioral ideas of learned overvaluation, and sociocultural claims about individualistic cultures. Evidence for rising narcissism across generations is debated.

People with NPD rarely seek treatment for narcissism itself; they come for depression or relationship problems. Therapy is difficult and the evidence is limited; therapists work on empathy, realistic self-appraisal and the distress behind the grandiosity.

SECTIONS.title: Personality disorders
ideas: A personality disorder is an enduring, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates from cultural expectations, begins by adolescence or early adulthood and causes distress or impairment. DSM-5-TR groups the ten disorders into three clusters.

Cluster A (odd or eccentric): paranoid (pervasive distrust), schizoid (detachment, restricted emotion) and schizotypal (odd beliefs and perceptions, eccentric behavior, social discomfort; related to schizophrenia).

Cluster B (dramatic, emotional, erratic): antisocial (disregard for others’ rights; age 18 or older with evidence of conduct disorder before 15), borderline (instability in relationships, self-image and mood, impulsivity, self-harm, fear of abandonment), histrionic (excessive emotion and attention-seeking) and narcissistic.

Cluster C (anxious or fearful): avoidant (feels inadequate, fears rejection), dependent (needs to be taken care of) and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (preoccupied with order, perfectionism and control; different from OCD, which has true obsessions and compulsions).

Treatment: dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), developed by Marsha Linehan, has the strongest support for borderline personality disorder; mentalization-based therapy also helps. Antisocial personality disorder responds poorly to treatment. DSM-5-TR Section III offers an alternative dimensional model rating personality functioning and traits.

SECTIONS.title: Disorders of childhood and adolescence
ideas: ADHD: inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity (6 or more symptoms in a category for children; 5 for ages 17 and older), present for at least 6 months, with several symptoms before age 12 and in two or more settings. Treated with stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) and behavioral parent training and classroom programs.

Autism spectrum disorder: persistent deficits in social communication and interaction plus restricted, repetitive behaviors, interests or sensory responses, present from early development. Severity levels 1–3 describe how much support is needed. Applied behavior analysis, communication training and supportive education help; vaccines do not cause autism.

Oppositional defiant disorder (angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behavior and vindictiveness for at least 6 months) and conduct disorder (repeated violation of others’ rights or major rules: aggression, destruction, deceit, serious rule-breaking). Early-onset conduct disorder can progress to antisocial personality disorder.

Also in the chapter: separation anxiety disorder, childhood depression and disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, enuresis and encopresis, specific learning disorder, and intellectual developmental disorder (deficits in intellectual and adaptive functioning beginning in the developmental period; severity is based on adaptive functioning, not IQ alone).
Children’s disorders are shaped by development: symptoms must be judged against what is normal for the child’s age, and treatment usually involves parents and schools.
